text: The respiratory system absorbs oxygen from the air and releases carbon dioxide from the blood; in chickens it also helps regulate body temperature by releasing heat. Birds do not breathe like mammals. Air enters through the glottis (which closes during swallowing to keep feed out of the lungs) and the trachea; where the trachea splits into two branches there is a voice box (syrinx) that lets roosters crow (hens can crow too, but normally don't, lacking the male hormones that encourage it). Air then reaches 9 air sacs — thin, colorless structures that inflate like tiny balloons inside the body cavity. The lungs handle gas exchange but cannot inflate themselves; it is the expansion and compression of the air sacs, driven by movement of the sternum and rib cage, that moves air in and out. Holding a bird too tightly (common when children hold chicks) restricts rib-cage movement and can suffocate it; overloading cages during transport has the same effect and is a cause of mortality, since the chicken cannot expand its breast to breathe.
